opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I think about it a lot. The core bottleneck in robot learning right now is data. Language models had the whole internet; we don't have an equivalent corpus of robot experience, so every hour of useful data has to be generated by an actual machine in the physical world. And humanoids are the most expensive, most fragile, hardest-to-maintain way to generate that data. You've got dozens of degrees of freedom, balance, hands that break, and when the robot falls over, someone has to pick it up and fix it. So your data per dollar is much worse than with a fixed arm on a table.

The bet people make, and I partly buy it, is that the human form is the right long-term target because the world is built for human bodies. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens were all designed around us. There's also a data argument for humanoids: if your robot is shaped like a person, you can potentially learn from the enormous amount of human video out there, and teleoperation becomes more intuitive because the operator's body maps onto the robot's. That retargeting story is one of the strongest reasons to go humanoid.

But I'd separate the long-term thesis from the near-term research strategy. If you go all-in on full humanoids today, you risk spending most of your effort on hardware reliability and locomotion rather than on the learning problem, which is where the real unlock is. A lot of the progress we've seen, cross-embodiment datasets, vision-language-action models, came from cheaper, simpler platforms that you could run in parallel and collect from at scale.

So my view is to hedge. Work on learning methods that are embodiment-agnostic, so data from arms, mobile manipulators, and humans all contributes to the same model. Then the humanoid becomes one more embodiment that benefits from everything else rather than a single point of failure. The biggest risk isn't that humanoids are the wrong form factor. It's betting your whole data flywheel on a platform that can't yet run reliably enough to feed it.

r001.rationale: The response says humanoids are expensive, fragile, and much worse in data per dollar than cheaper, simpler platforms that can run in parallel, identifying the difficulty of matching their data-collection scale.

r002.rationale: It says robot learning needs data at scale, but does not state that scale is necessary to encounter problems that arise at scale.

r003.rationale: It describes hardware reliability and locomotion as obstacles that can consume effort and keep humanoids from running reliably enough to supply data at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about constantly, because the humanoid form factor is really a bet that the data problem resolves in a particular way.

So the honest framing is this. When we did RT-1, RT-2 at Google, the bottleneck was never the model architecture. It was that we had, I think, 130,000 demonstrations collected over seventeen months with a fleet of thirteen robots. That's a staggering amount of human effort for what in language model terms is a rounding error. Language models get to train on the internet. Robots get to train on whatever you physically went and collected. And every embodiment you add, every new gripper or arm or body, fragments that data further.

So there's a reasonable critique that says, why would you pick the hardest, most expensive, most unstable form factor when you can't even saturate data for a two-fingered arm on a table? And I take that seriously. A humanoid is more actuators, more failure modes, more ways to collect garbage data because the robot fell over.

But here's the case for it. The thing that made RT-2 interesting was that the robot could inherit knowledge from vision-language pretraining. Internet data transferred into robot behavior, at least somewhat. And if you believe that's the dominant source of scaling, then the question becomes: which body makes that transfer easiest? The internet is full of humans doing things with human bodies in human environments. Every YouTube video of someone cooking, every egocentric dataset, that's all implicitly humanoid data. A humanoid is the form factor with the smallest embodiment gap to the largest free dataset on earth.

The other piece is that data at scale, in the long run, is not going to come from teleoperators in a lab. It's going to come from deployment. And deployment means the robot has to be useful in the world as it already exists, with stairs, doors, and tools designed for us. A humanoid can go into a warehouse or a home without anyone redesigning the space. That's what unlocks a flywheel where robots in the field generate the data for the next model, which is the only data story that actually looks like the language model story.

So the risk I'd flag isn't really "humanoid versus arm." It's whether you can survive the gap. There's a stretch where the hardware is expensive, the data is thin, the models aren't good enough to be deployed, and you're burning capital waiting for the flywheel to start. Companies die in that gap. My assessment is that the bet is right on the long time horizon and genuinely dangerous on the short one. And the way you manage it is you're very disciplined about picking tasks where you can get real deployment data early, even if they're narrow, rather than demoing general-purpose capability that isn't backed by scale yet.

r001.rationale: The response calls humanoids a harder, more expensive form factor and contrasts their data burden with collecting data for a two-fingered arm, identifying the difficulty of scaling data collection as a risk.

r002.rationale: It argues that deployment can generate data for future models, but does not state that data collection at scale is needed to encounter problems that arise at scale.

r003.rationale: The response describes data and deployment challenges, but does not characterize achieving scale with humanoid robots as an engineering problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the need for data at scale is both the opportunity and a source of risk. You need robots interacting with the world to learn, but you don’t want collecting that experience to expose people to systems that aren’t reliable yet. So I would separate the ambition of a general-purpose humanoid from how you actually develop and deploy it.

You can start in constrained environments, with human supervision, limits on force and speed, and clear ways to stop the robot. Then expand what it’s allowed to do as you gather evidence that it can handle those situations safely. The important thing isn’t just how much data you collect; it’s whether that data covers failures and whether the robot can recognize when it needs help.

There’s also a privacy question. If robots are learning in spaces where people live and work, what they observe can be sensitive. So consent and decisions about what gets recorded have to be part of the data strategy from the beginning.

I wouldn’t treat the need for scale as a reason to relax those constraints. I’d treat it as a reason to build a development process where you can learn a lot while keeping the consequences of mistakes small.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the need for data at scale but does not identify difficulty matching inexpensive platforms such as ALOHA as a humanoid-robot risk.

r002.rationale: It says robots need real-world interaction to learn, but does not state that scale is necessary to encounter problems that arise at scale.

r003.rationale: It proposes a constrained development process, but does not characterize achieving scale with humanoid robots as an engineering problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the risks of collecting data from the risks of deploying the robot. We need a lot of data, but that doesn’t mean putting a robot in someone’s home and letting it learn through trial and error. You can collect demonstrations through teleoperation, work in controlled environments, and gradually expand what the robot is allowed to do as you understand its failure modes.

The physical aspect matters a lot. A model giving a bad answer and a robot making an unexpected movement have very different consequences. So you need safety mechanisms that don’t depend on the learned policy always being correct—limits on force and speed, ways to stop the robot, and human supervision appropriate to the task.

And then there’s privacy. If the data comes from homes or workplaces, you have to think carefully about consent and what you’re recording. For me, the question is how we get useful, diverse data while keeping the collection process safe. Scale is necessary, but scale by itself isn’t evidence that a robot is ready to operate autonomously around people.

r001.rationale: The response says a lot of data is needed, but does not mention inexpensive platforms such as ALOHA or the difficulty of matching their data-collection scale with humanoid robots.

r002.rationale: It calls scale necessary, but does not state that scale is needed to encounter problems that arise at scale.

r003.rationale: It discusses collection methods and safety measures, but does not characterize achieving scale with humanoid robots as an engineering problem.
